lesson.title: Same Blueprint, Different Buildings: Comparative Anatomy
lesson.summary: Comparative anatomy is the study of similarities and differences in body structures across species, and it reveals that shared structure can come from two very different sources: inheritance from a common ancestor, or independent adaptation to similar demands.
lesson.body:
Long before DNA sequencing existed, naturalists had already noticed something striking simply by dissecting and comparing animals: many species that look completely different on the outside, and that live in wildly different ways, share a strikingly similar underlying structure. Comparative anatomy is the systematic study of these anatomical similarities and differences across species. It became one of the central lines of evidence for evolution because the patterns it reveals are hard to explain any other way.

This kind of comparison only makes sense once you remember what these organisms are built from in the first place. All the animals compared in this chapter, humans, whales, bats, birds, cats, are built from eukaryotic cells sharing the same basic cellular architecture: a nucleus, similar organelles, the same basic machinery for reading DNA and building proteins. That shared cellular foundation is itself a first, deep layer of evidence for common ancestry, and it is what makes it possible for very different looking bodies to still be assembled from a shared underlying developmental and genetic toolkit, expressed differently in different lineages.

The single most famous example in comparative anatomy is the vertebrate limb. Look at the forelimb skeleton of a human arm, a whale's flipper, a bat's wing, a cat's leg, and a bird's wing side by side, and despite being used for entirely different purposes, grasping and manipulating objects, swimming, flying, walking, flying again by a completely different route, all of them are built from the same basic set of bones in the same basic arrangement: a single bone closest to the body, two bones next, a cluster of small wrist bones, then digits extending outward. Biologists call this the pentadactyl, or five digit, limb pattern. There is no functional reason a wing needs the same bone layout as a leg or an arm, wings could in principle be built many different ways, and in fact, as the next two chapters will show, other flying animals built their wings on a completely different plan.

Comparative anatomy raises an important question that the next several chapters answer directly: when two species share a similar structure, how do you tell whether that similarity reflects true shared ancestry or just a coincidental solution to a similar problem? The answer turns out to depend on what is beneath the surface, the underlying architecture and developmental origin, not just the outward function. Structures that share underlying structure because of common ancestry are called homologous structures. Structures that share only outward function, having evolved that similarity independently, are called analogous structures. Distinguishing between the two, and understanding why the distinction matters, is the subject of the next two chapters, with a further variation, vestigial structures, covered right after.
